title: The Korean War: The Forgotten War

cards.h: A war that never officially ended
cards.b:
The Korean War was fought from June 1950 to July 1953. It ended with an armistice, not a peace treaty, so the two Koreas are still technically at war. Its cost in lives was enormous, and its shape still defines East Asia.

The war showed how the Cold War could turn hot. It also shows how a civil conflict can become a global struggle.

On 25 June 1950 North Korean forces crossed the 38th parallel into the South. They took Seoul within days. The UN Security Council called for help, and the United States led a UN force to defend South Korea.

Historians argue about the start of the war. Soviet archives opened in the 1990s show that Kim Il Sung had won Stalin's approval for an attack, though Stalin wanted to avoid direct Soviet involvement.

In September 1950 General Douglas MacArthur landed at Inchon, behind North Korean lines. The attack cut the enemy supply lines, and UN forces drove north. They reached the Yalu river, on the border with China, by late October.

The advance triggered a Chinese intervention in October and November 1950. The Chinese army pushed back across the 38th parallel, and the war became a long, bloody stalemate.

Bruce Cumings, The Korean War: A History (2010)

Cumings argues that the origins of the war lay in the civil conflict within Korea and in the division of the country after 1945. He stresses that both sides had local goals.

His view is controversial, but it is a useful correction to the simple picture of an invasion from nowhere.
The war lasted three years and one month. The armistice line near the 38th parallel is still the basis of the demilitarised zone.

Peace talks began in 1951 at Kaesong and later moved to Panmunjom. The talks dragged on for two years, mainly over the exchange of prisoners and the line of the front. Meanwhile the fighting continued, with trenches, hills and heavy losses.

The armistice was signed on 27 July 1953. No peace treaty was ever signed, and the DMZ still divides the peninsula.

The Korean War is often taught as a simple act of aggression by the communist North, stopped by the free world. The story is clear and easy to remember.

Historians argue the picture is more complex. The Korean civil conflict, the Soviet and Chinese roles, the US decisions and the politics of the UN all shaped the war. Each side had its own reasons, and each made mistakes.

Estimates of the dead run to about two to three million people, including civilians on both sides. Cities were destroyed, and many families were split by the border. The war left Korea divided and scarred.

The war also changed the United States, which kept troops in Korea and Japan for decades. It helped set the pattern for the Cold War in Asia.

The Korean War is often called the forgotten war, because it came between the Second World War and Vietnam. It received less attention in the West, though it was among the most intense conflicts of the Cold War.

Historians argue about why the war is less remembered. The reasons include the late 1950s focus on other crises, and the lack of a clear victory. Its memory is strongest in Korea itself.

cards.h: Prisoners and the choice of home
cards.b:
At the end of the war, many prisoners refused to return to the side that had held them. The question of repatriation nearly derailed the armistice. Over 20,000 prisoners chose not to go back to North Korea or China.

The problem was handled by a neutral commission. It was the Indian army that took charge of the custody of the prisoners.

India played an unusual role in the Korean War. Krishna Menon, the Indian envoy at the UN, pushed for a compromise. In 1953 India agreed to chair a Neutral Nations Repatriation Commission and provided a custodian force to hold the prisoners.

The Indian general K. S. Thimayya led the custodian force. The operation was a great test of neutrality in the Cold War. India's role showed how a newly independent country could shape world events.

Five things to remember
  1. The war ran from June 1950 to July 1953.
  2. Inchon (September 1950) turned the war.
  3. China entered in October 1950.
  4. The armistice was signed at Panmunjom on 27 July 1953.
  5. India chaired the prisoner repatriation commission.
Think about it
  • Why was the war never formally ended by a peace treaty?
  • Can a neutral country do useful work in a war?
